source.title_on_document: AI use in American newspapers is widespread, uneven, and rarely disclosed

paper_design_summary: The authors run the Pangram AI-text detector over three corpora of published U.S. newspaper articles: 186,507 articles from 1,528 newspapers (June-September 2025), 44,803 opinion pieces from the NYT, WaPo, and WSJ (August 2022-September 2025), and 20,132 articles by 10 reporters before and after ChatGPT. The outcome is the share of articles labeled AI-generated or mixed, broken down by circulation, ownership, topic, language, and time, plus manual audits of disclosure and hallucinations. No person is assigned to AI and no creativity or diversity outcome is measured.

eligibility.reason: Detection audit of published newspaper articles. No people are assigned to AI, there are no participants, and the only outcome is the detector-labeled share of AI text. The paper has no creativity, novelty, similarity, or diversity outcome (the cosine-similarity clustering on p. 20 only groups republished duplicates to count AI labels among them). The codebook excludes studies that measure how much AI text exists with no diversity outcome, so it does not qualify as observational context either.

one_line_finding: Pangram labels 9.1 percent of 186K recent U.S. newspaper articles as AI-generated (5.2 percent) or mixed (3.9 percent) (p. 4, Section 3.1; Table 1, p. 3), with higher rates in small local papers and in NYT/WaPo/WSJ opinion pieces (4.56 vs 0.71 percent, Table 11, p. 23), and 96.5 percent of authors in a 200-article audit did not disclose AI use (p. 6).
notes: No outcome bears on with_ai, across_people, or after_ai, so the outcomes lists are empty. Outcomes the paper reports, all excluded from the form: detector-labeled AI share by circulation, state, topic, ownership, language and year (Figures 1-4, 8-15, 18-24; Tables 1, 11, 13); disclosure audit of 200 articles (Table 2, p. 6); hallucination audit of 100 AI-labeled vs 100 human-labeled articles, 41 vs 5 percent (p. 7); machine-translation robustness (Table 10); AI quotes within articles (pp. 19-20); AI labels among republished duplicate clusters formed by cosine similarity >= 0.85 (p. 20). Qualitative remarks that AI-assisted articles have more em dashes and fewer specific details (p. 17, Table 6) are examples, not a measured diversity or creativity outcome. The candidate record's library label 'Corpus' and theme 'Academic & scientific writing' do not match the document, which studies newspapers.
